That's PLENTY! ;-)

I'll throw out the first comment, since I'm here...

Sigh...I'm going to miss the table restructuring cards. Stupidly, I
never used them enough but I thought they made the game interesting
that they even existed. Even so, I'm not shocked that they should be
banned: they _were_ very powerful cards and I find the suggestion that
they might be considered "not suited for competive play" palatable.
I don't know if I'd call them "unbalanced" or "broken", exactly, though.

Succubus Club, as I commented when it was previously discussed, hadn't
been abused or broken in my part of the world. Apparently, it must have
been causing a problem elsewhere. It still seems a bit premature to me
to ban it, but again, the suggestion that it's "not suited for competitive
play" strikes me as being arguable. Wholesale trading of cards in hand
and permanents is a pretty extreme mechanic given how the game is
otherwise play. I won't really miss it.

Both of these mechanics are actually pretty extreme. It leaves me to
wonder if we might them recreated in other cards in the future. In
the case of position-switching, perhaps it might reappear with a higher
cost, more limitations, more difficult to use or what not. In the case
of permanent and/or card trading, perhaps it might be reborn in a milder
form - perhaps a card that would allow two players to trade one single
permanent for one other single permanent once per turn, for instance (or
one card in hand for one card in hand).

Fred (nope, it's not April - can't be April Fools...)

Well, one thing good about it: I've been bitching these last few months
about how the game tends to discourage pro-active fast decks. Good
players inevitably seems to play a lot of reaction because it allows
them to build up their strength slowly with permanents and pool gain.
If you try to take your prey out fast the moment you're out of the gate,
you better be able to deliver the death blow VERY fast because if you
don't, your prey starts walling up and the rest of the table immediately
begins to gang up on you since _they're_ all playing slow build-up
games too. The chance someone would find a way to pass a Dramatic
Upheavel and "steal" the oust you've been working on was just one more
thing in that pattern. And least that's one thing you won't have to
worry about any more.

Fred

> The Banned List is expanded to include three cards that are

> Restructure, and Succubus Club.

Well, now for my comments.
There is a lot of luck involved in playing V:tES in a tournament
environment. One part of that is seating order. I liked the cards that
change seating order because in that way players were able to "change their
luck". These cards are political actions so they are easily stopped by a
delayed tactics and votes around the table.
As for Succubus Club, I never liked that card. It supported table split
deals and deals in general. Deals are a good portion of the "social" part of
the game but are abused in tournaments, as they allow a bad deck with a
talkative player to end up way better. As we have seen in the "Silence of
Death" tournament at the EC in Heidelberg, not to talk during games also has
a special quality.
Well, let愀 see how things work out without these cards.

'Cause with table switch votes:

A) Mean that it is pointless to spend all your effort trying to whittle your
prey down to near dead, 'cause someone across the table, who you can't

Messages.Author: Jozxyqk
Messages.Body:
LSJ <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote:

> The Banned List is expanded to include three cards that are
> not suited for competitive play: Dramatic Upheaval, Kindred
> Restructure, and Succubus Club.

(This response was originally a lot more coherent, but it
got eaten before it got posted; reconstructing it from memory)

Banning Succubus Club, I don't care one way or the other.

But banning Dramatic Upheaval and Kindred Restructure?
I'm not personally too happy with that one.

I can see all the points in favor of banning DU and KR.
You're never quite sure who your prey is.
You can hop over and "steal" a VP.
It makes "play to win" a lot greyer to judge.

*However*, I also see DU (and to a lesser extent, KR) as
having legitimate defensive strategies. I'm sure many of
you would agree that there is some merit in using it to
"get away from" a predator that your deck simply wasn't
built to handle. It's part of the knowledge of the deck.
With DU banned, it means that you'll have to otherwise
devote more deckspace to handling a larger variety of
predators. (which, in a dedicated vote deck, is already
a pretty tight space)

I would much more have preferred a rewording of DU (and,
sure, ban KR if you must), than outright banning it.
Either that, or changing the VEKN scoring rules
mathematically, so that VP-stealing is somehow discouraged
(this second option is much harder).

Here's a simple example of a reword (don't harp on the
specifics too much, I'm just pointing out that it *could* be
changed with clear text):

Dramatic Upheaval
Political Action
Choose any other Methuselah.
Successful referendum means you switch places with that
Methuselah, end your minion phase, and put this card into
play.
The next time you gain a Victory Point, the chosen Methuselah
gains that Victory Point instead (even if that Methuselah was
already ousted) and burn this card.

I hope that Monocle of Clarity can serve as a precedent that
useful cards with questionable rulings can find their way
back off of the banned list.

changing the cards).

> Either that, or changing the VEKN scoring rules
> mathematically, so that VP-stealing is somehow discouraged
> (this second option is much harder).

VP-sniping is only one aspect of the problem.

> Here's a simple example of a reword (don't harp on the
> specifics too much, I'm just pointing out that it *could* be
> changed with clear text):
>
> Dramatic Upheaval
> Political Action
> Choose any other Methuselah.
> Successful referendum means you switch places with that
> Methuselah, end your minion phase, and put this card into
> play.
> The next time you gain a Victory Point, the chosen Methuselah
> gains that Victory Point instead (even if that Methuselah was
> already ousted) and burn this card.

If that had been implemented instead of the ban, we'd now be
talking about why not just ban it instead of wallpaper the
card *and* increase the errata count.

(That's the larger "we", BTW -- not just the two of us in
isolation.)

> I hope that Monocle of Clarity can serve as a precedent that
> useful cards with questionable rulings can find their way
> back off of the banned list.

Absolutely. That avenue is always a possibility.

Some cards, like ante cards for example, would be very difficult
to re-word. Seat changers are similarly disadvantaged, given
the nature of changing seats.

Messages.Author: Aramis
Messages.Body:
Damn.

While I figured that Succubus Club was going to get some sort of
treatment I didn't think it would get banned outright. I really liked
Succubus Club. As a player who enjoys the RPG background of the game,
I thought the card gave the game its flavor of the clandestine deals
and backroom negotiations of ancient Methuselahs. Also as a dedicated
Assamite player I lament losing the one card that allowed me to play
the clan in character with the RPG as hired assassins. As Kevin
Mergen alluded to in an earlier thread on Succubus Club, I have
regularly used the card in my tournament level Assamite decks to
extort protection money, arrange hits, and negotiate non-aggression
pacts. It's a shame that such a useful and characterful card has to
be banned because a few people used it spitefully to throw a game or
king-make.

I don't think banning Succubus Club really solves anything though. No
one puts it in their deck with the intention of throwing the game or
kingmaking. Like myself they probably have very good legitimate uses
for the Club in mind, after all a Master slot is never something you
can afford to just waste on a whim. The problem isn't Succubbus Club,
it's bad players. A player that bleeds/PTOs/torporizes minions
cross-table for spite is just as disruptive to the table, but we don't
ban Kindred Spirits, PTO, or (D) rush cards. Too make a bad analogy:
it's not guns that kill people, it's people who kill people. The gun
(Succubus Club) is not the problem, the problem is that people are
spiteful.

I don't understand why Succubus Club got such a narrow fix to it in
CE. Had the problem been addressed by putting a cap on how much you
can transfer (1 card for 1 card, no more than 10 pool) I think the
card would have been well-limited and still very useful for those of
us with legitimate uses in mind. I don't expect these arguments are
anything new or that anything will change as a result of my words
here, but I just have to post my lament this sad, sad day.

David "Aramis" Buerger
PS. The loss of table-switch votes is also very disappointing, but not
nearly as close to home. Although I imagine it is of much greater
importance to the game and will have far greater reprecussions than
the loss of Succubus Club.

LSJ [fantasy]: Per definition no. A card that changes your prey doesnt

undermine the predator-prey relationship more than a card that
rearranges the table. Why should the predator-prey relationship from

acting against it.

Making master cards that let votes pass automatically, and then weaken

Creating new winning strategies (depleting the deck of your prey) and
then killing one game strategie doesnt look right.

>Like other people have said there are a lot of other cards that undermine

>the pred-prey relationship. Premium example : Eagle愀 Sight. But that愀 not

This "premium" example is incorrect.

After playing Eagle's Sight, your prey and predator remain the same.

This means that while it is possible to play Eagle's Sight and block
cross-table actions, you still have to oust your prey to gain VP and to
win. Eagle's Sight is a useful tool to prevent others from assisting
your prey or predator (ill-timed Political Strangleholds or Ancient
Influences, for example), but it now must be used to support ousting
your own prey if you want to win.

DU and KR, on the other hand, allow you to change (ie. undermine) the
predator/prey relationships that are set at the start of the game...
meaning that it's a better plan to sit, bloat, and wait for someone to
get low, and then snipe their VP. This means each deck must pack plenty
of Delaying Tactics (DI is insufficient, as Charming Lobby "hides" the
DU from DI), and have it in hand when they go for the oust, or lose.

>the problem. I think that undermination of the pred-prey relationship IS the

>foundation of V:TES. It愀 not the tunnel game it is a game of intriguing

>politics. Banning KR and DU just seems random to me.

Garfield's intent was to create a multiplayer game that wasn't just
"gang up on the leader", as all other multiplayer games are. V:TES has
become a game of "gang up on the leader", and has suffered greatly for
it. Removing KR and DU mean that political decks are just going to have
to oust their prey like all the rest of us, instead of disrupting and
stalling the game while waiting for someone to get low.

A political deck that just sits and waits to snipe *IS* disrupting the
table balance; its prey runs free, its grandpredator runs free.

Messages.Author: Wes
Messages.Body:
"Johannes Walch" <joha...@scram.de> wrote

>
> Like other people have said there are a lot of other cards that undermine

> the pred-prey relationship. Premium example : Eagle愀 Sight.

I disagree that Eagle's Sight _undermines_ the effect. It merely steps
outside of it briefly. It is a transient effect and generally used to hurt
your prey, which is the very essence of predator-prey.

Most of the cards that *can* be targeted elsewhere on the table (Bum's Rush,
Kindred Spirits, etc) are also transient effects. There is little point
targeting your grandpredator with Kindred Spirits if you do not have a means
of taking advantage of it later, ie switching seats.

As a result of this change, the potential of such cards to be disruptive to
the predator-prey relationship has been indirectly weakened. But that's
acceptable to me.

Basically, the banning of DU and KR is going to force every player's head to
look left a bit more, and that will result in better games in the long run.
Probably faster games also, which I'm very much in favour of. I don't think
it's been mentioned yet, but the discussions caused by DU and KR refrendums
are some of the longest and most time-wasting. Not to mention the disruption
of actually moving cards physically. I imagine we'll see fewer timed-out
games as a result of this change.

> Of course. I meant a probably more ordered discussion where you can
> actually
> identify a consensus.

I'm actually surprised by the negative reaction to this ruling. I've been in
many a discussion where people felt that DU and KR were bad for the game. Of
course, many more were about PTO, but that card is also _slightly_ weakened
by this change.

Another option?

"Choose a Methusalah. If this referendum is successful, switch seating
with that Methusalah and put this card into play with X counters,
where X is the number of Methusalahs in the game. During your untap,
remove a counter. When this card has zero counters, burn it. While
this card is in play, if your Prey is ousted you get 0 (or 0.5?) VP."

Or alternately...

"Choose a Methusalah. If this referendum is successful, switch seating
with that Methusalah and put this card into play. During your untap,
put a counter on this card. When this card has X counters (where X is
the number of Methusalahs in the game, burn it. While this card is in
play, if your Prey is ousted you get 0 (or 0.5?) VP."

The second one allows the timespan to be shortened if other people
make kills. But both will still not net any (full?) VP to a quick
snipe. Moving to get a softer prey, or to get away from a harder
predator, would both still be ideal uses of the card. Similar time
displacement usage for Kindred Restructure would allow putting the
Stealth Bleeder behind the Wall deck, or the Bruise Bleeder behind
your Predator. If you have to be around for 3-6 turns, does this not
re-establish the predator/prey mechanic somewhat?

massive damage turn could oust someone without a DI or DT in hand.
* Practically: the above 3 cards turn the game into a discussion match.
I've seen games where between the playing of the vote and the actual
changing of seats there was 20-30 minutes of discussion. And the actual
changing itself takes time too.

* Why IMO this will not make vote decks unplayable: simply because other
people will play less Delaying Tactics in their decks. Most decks only pack
it against 2 things: seat changers and PTO. And I think this will be better
for the game too. I've seen to many finals where every deck was packing 3-4
DI and 2-4 Delaying tactics. And they're booooooooooooooring as hell.

* Maybe vote decks will now start playing attrition decks too instead of
defending until they can get a shot a an easy oust?

Just my .02
Jeroen

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Daneel wrote:

> Well, that's a bit overgeneralized. If you can kill someone on 9 pool, why
> don't you kill your prey?

'Cause if it is easier to kill someone elses pry than it is yours, for
whatever reason, table switch votes let you. Removing them from the
environment says "You have to kill your own prey--do your own hard work",
which is a lot closer to the main theme of the game--kill your prey.

> It's more a problem with leaving your prey on 1-2 pool

Which is, ya know, less than 10, making my point not invalid.

Peter D Bakija

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Mochuda wrote:

> Well bums's rush (and any rush card) should be banished too as someone
> can rush me crosstable and undermine my relations with my prey/predator

You don't gain VP's by Rushing cross table. In fact, more often that not,
Rushing cross table makes you *lose* VPs ('cause it usually compromises your
position and strengthens someone elses, providing built in disincentive to
Rush cross table).

Table switch votes got you VPs off of someone elses hard work. Now you just
have to do your own work.



Messages.Body:
Mochuda <moc...@arfe.netNOSPAM> wrote in message news:<41b1e9a7$0$579$79c1...@nan-newsreader-07.noos.net>...
> <snip>
>
> >> Care to explain why these cards were banned? I cannot see any apparent
> >> reason.
> >
> >
> > Not suited to competitive play, since they undermine the foundation
> > of the game (namely, the predator-prey relationship).
> >
>
> <snip>

>
> Well bums's rush (and any rush card) should be banished too as someone
> can rush me crosstable and undermine my relations with my prey/predator
>

No, they don't. You still have the same predator and prey. So what's
changed there?

> and eagle sight, sensory deprivation, temptation... too

Rubbish. The abiltiy to engage/interact outside the default
relationship is something different. It does not change the facts
about your predator and prey.

>
> really I don't get the point
> banishing DU and KR is just making S&B far easier as these decks won't
> have to care about table vision

Oh, and they cared sooo much about it before?

I think that you overestimate the average S&B player.

> and vote decks lose the main edge

I disagree. They lose one strategy, but there zare still plenty more
existing options, not too mention upcoming expansions.
>
> vote is a hard strategy as it requires some skills and a good flow in
> playing cards (i need the vote, eventually to stealth it by, then I need
> vote lock or to negociate with the one who has it)
> So this strategy should be able to do something other strategies are not
> able too, and that is place switch.
> Yes it is a powerful strategy but they are *SO MANY* things that can
> spoil it and that is actually what the game is all about !
>
> Now what... Just play KRCs ? really nice...
>

No, actually you get a couple of more cards, other than KRC....

Cheers

Messages.Author: Mike
Messages.Body:
"LSJ" <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote in message
news:8bisd.88887$7i4....@bgtnsc05-news.ops.worldnet.att.net...

> > Care to explain why these cards were banned? I cannot see any apparent
> > reason.
>
> Not suited to competitive play, since they undermine the foundation
> of the game (namely, the predator-prey relationship).

Is it possible for you to please share which cases were used as a basis of
evidence? AFAICS DU and KR do not undermine or obviate the predator-prey
relationship, they simply define a new predator-prey relationship. Certainly
the threat of DU and KR is nothing compared to Anarch Revolt, a dangerous
stackable card which has effect which clearly *does* defy the predator-prey
relationship, and yet which has *still* not been touched despite, numerous,
repeated requests from members of the V:TES community.

In addition, DU and KR is a key defence for voting decks against
hammer-bleed or weenie-rush type decks. The ban now makes voting even
weaker, certainly a step back for the meta-game, not a step forward.

> > Who decides which cards are getting banned?
>
> The V:EKN.

I don't remember seeing an reference to a consultation process, although
that certainly would have been nice.

> There are. Such discussions are nearly continuous, here, in email,
> on forums, on chats, face to face, etc.

I don't recall seeing any proposals to ban DU and KR in the public domain
before now. Could you provide some references?

> Those opinions are taken into account.

I'd like to formally voice my own disappointment too.

> Surely you realize that there are others who work countless hours.
> And they do not all step lockstep all the time on all issues.

True. However in this case, given enough time, it entirely possible that we
will be the majority.

Regards,

Mike Nudd
VEKN Prince of London

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <cafbc9c8.04120...@posting.google.com>, Enrique
San Mart?n <es...@chile.com> writes:
>The argument of the "undermine the prey-predator mechanic" (UtPPM)
>it's very poor, because:
>
>Allmost in vtes it's undermine (or overuled), many card's give the
>posibily to do things that can't be done with the basic of the rules.

True, but you're missing the point that LSJ (and the V:EKN) appear to
view the predator-prey dynamic a fundamental part of the framework of
the game.

Keeping that *framework* in tact is a very different argument to doing
things that the basic rules don't give you the possibility to do (e.g.
steal a location).

As an extreme example, imagine a vote that said: "Pick a Methuselah.
That Methuselah is ousted. You gain the victory point and pool (if
any)." Clearly, that vote undermines the fundamental dynamics of the
game. (If you disagree with that, I think we'll have issues agreeing at
all, ever.)

And hence maintaining the framework is rather different to the actual
possibilities that are/should be allowed inside that framework.

(I still don't know what I think of the change. But arguments like this
one are unlikely to cause V:EKN to shift, IMO.)

--
James Coupe

EBD690ECD7A1FB457CA2 Designing a deck that just calls votes.
13D7E668C3695D623D5D That's crazy talk, there.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <41b38c66$0$29750$ed2e...@ptn-nntp-reader04.plus.net>, Mike

<mi...@vekn.org.uk> writes:
>Is it possible for you to please share which cases were used as a basis of
>evidence? AFAICS DU and KR do not undermine or obviate the predator-prey
>relationship, they simply define a new predator-prey relationship.

Consider:

You, me, LSJ, Peter Bakija and Rob Treasure sit down at a table, in that
order.

Throughout the flow of the game, each of us is discarding chaff, looking
at the table, working out our defences and so on. Peter knows that LSJ
wants to oust him, and is trying to form tentative alliances with both
you and me. Ditto, the rest of the table, where it makes sense.

Peter is playing a rush deck, with some bleed backup. Sadly, Rob
Treasure is playing a toolbox Tzimisce War Ghoul deck, so Peter is in
real trouble. Lots of people are trying to work out how the table
dynamic is going to go, where they need to balance things out, whether
they can still get a table win if LSJ gets Peter. LSJ has got Peter
down to 2 pool, though. Peter is manfully trying to take out LSJ's
weenies, though it's hard work. He might go next turn, he might not.
His defences are okay - but will they be good enough?

I'm having major trouble getting through LSJ, though. He's playing
weenie stealth bleed, with a butt-load of Tribute to the Master. I
throw damage after damage at him, and he can soak it all.

Everyone knows the state of the table, everyone knows who's who. Peter
is working at the moment on defending against LSJ and Rob, not you and
me.

Now, as it happens, I happen to draw my Dramatic Upheaval this turn. I
play it and luckily it passes. Now, this *could* have been Vox Domini-
ed or Delaying Tactics-ed. But it's not. After all, Peter saw LSJ
playing some stealth bleed and Rob playing War Ghoul toolbox, so vote
defence wasn't top of his list of priorities. And he was doing
relatively badly, so one of us deciding to vanquish him wasn't likely -
it'd just help LSJ.

I swap places with LSJ.

I now oust Peter with a single KRC.

1) What could Peter have done to defend against that?

2) Should everyone on a table be thinking "What happens if the table
suddenly becomes a completely different order?" every time they play a
card?

Messages.Author: Ector
Messages.Body:
LSJ <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote in message news:<41B11E2D...@white-wolf.com>...
> The nature of "randomness" in determining seating is clarified a bit.
>
> The Banned List is expanded to include three cards that are
> not suited for competitive play: Dramatic Upheaval, Kindred
> Restructure, and Succubus Club.

Metagame predictions:
* Voting decks are much weaker (as though Rastacouriere isn't enough).
DU and KR were the primary "shelters" of voting decks against, say,
fast-bleeding decks or rush decks. You feel that you're going to die
here, so you make the effort to find a better place. Future voting
decks would have to pack more bounce and combat protection cards.
* Intercept decks are much stronger. Intercepting neighbour is
generally a nightmare for a voting deck, if it doesn't have enough
stealth to beat the intercept, and now the voting deck cannot even
convince the interceptor to pass the KR or DU and become allies after
it.
* Rush decks are stronger. Voting decks have to pack political
actions, vote-pushing, stealth or "cannot block" cards etc. etc., so
they cannot regularly pose a serious threat in combat. Rush predator
can methodically kill voting vampires one by one - his prey can't
escape anymore.

That's all. I'm not going to say that the metagame shift would be
bad...and it definitely can be fixed with new cards.

Ector

You can see how much of a consensus can be reached by the "public" these
days by simply reading the newsgroup. Most people will never change
their opinions, and the most noise is typically made by the people who
have the least qualification to make that noise.

Closed-door "IC" type of things have been the way to get things done
since time immemorial, both in your country, mine, and many others --
because the more people you involve in a decision-making process, the
less actually gets decided. Limiting the number of people involved is
the only way to be certain that all avenues actually GET explored, and
that those people don't completely get derailed by having to perpetually
re-cover ground that has already been decided.

One of my tasks at work is to sit down with the technical support groups
and discuss the most common issues/calls they are receiving, and from
that determine whether or not changes need to be made to the product.
These meetings consist of only a few people from Support, instead of the
entire Support staff -- because we want to actually get things done.

If I had to address each individual Support person's concerns, I would
spend all my time weeding out the 90% or so requests that were trivial
or incorrect, and I would never get anything done. The few Support
people I DO speak to do all that for me, and present only the 10% or so
that are serious concerns -- and THOSE get discussed at length.

A similar parallel exists in V:TES. The complaints from players all get
registered, both in person, on the forums, and everywhere... then those
complaints get filtered by priority appropriately, along with the
garbage reasons for the otherwise-sound complaints, and then discussion
commences on those sound complaints.

possibly two. HI GUYS! * HUG! *)

That's a rather conservative response. In terms of metagame theory the
predator-prey relationship means that you should only be able to oust your
prey, not other methuselahs around the table. A DU or a KR will give you a
new prey, but the general relationships from predator to prey around the
table are preserved.

The only point of contention as James Coupe has noted above (in the thread)
is the point of timing where the vote is called and the new prey-to-be may
or may not be able to react in their own defence. And as I've noted above
(in the thread) this could be safely cushioned with errata such that once a
DU or KR has been played (whether successful or not) that Methuselah's
minion phase immediately ends. This give not just the new prey but *the
whole table* a turn to adjust and respond before the offending player can
act again - this should make stealing a end-game kill a lot harder, whilst
still allowing the table dynamic to be changed.

kind of play. I realise that having to deal with this kind of play at all is
an issue in any case, but less for some than others. I would argue though
that DU/KR isn't *always* played in the late game to steal a kill. The issue
regarding timing could be resolved with errata in any case, *not* a total
ban - e.g. once a DU or KR has been played successfully (whether it fails or
passes) that methuselah's minion phase immediately ends.

> 2) Should everyone on a table be thinking "What happens if the table
> suddenly becomes a completely different order?" every time they play a
> card?

Not every time cards are played, but when a strong vote deck is on the
table, I've always considered that an issue. But then again I usually play
with intercept coming out of my ass which means it's never really been that
much of an issue for me personally :)

> 3) If table-switching is such a crucial element of the game, why is it
> only available to political decks? (Many other forms of offence and
> defence - pool destruction, minion denial, secondary resource
> manipulation etc. - are available to many, many deck types.)

That is a good question, but I would argue that making similar options
available to other kinds of decks (Anarchs? Black Hand?) would be far more
interesting than banning the existing cards and removing the possibility of
the strategy altogether. We should bear in mind that in V:TES the available
strategies are very small: bleeding, fighting or voting. Deck milling is now
a possible fourth, but it's very much an outside, unlikely case that you'd
score a table win. Anything that creates more options and variety is IMHO a
good thing.

> I am vaguely undecided on these points, though believe that these points
> are somewhat fundamental to the change that's been enacted.

Perhaps the most serious complaint (which I didn't raise before but which
I've seen elsewhere) is how come after 10 years of V:TES, and DU and KR
being available for the *entire* period should they be banned now? If they
were such a problem then they should have been banned before - what changed
in the last year or so that has made a ban so necessary all of a sudden?
I've never seen people bitching about them in the public domain to the
extent that a ban would need to be mooted. On this basis alone it strikes me
as rather unecessary...? *shrugs*

GREAT!

plenty of options to balanec the table.

was oustable), is likely going to be harder to oust.

our play. If the game goes 4 hours, so be it.

>questionable in any case under 'playing to win' remit.

I think the first part of this is highly questionable.

Vote decks can throw damage cross-table. Rush decks can throw rushes
cross-table, which certainly can contribute to the oust significantly
even if it doesn't do it itself. Add Fame, if you need the actual
killing blow.

Some bleed decks can go cross-table. A number of them can go upstream
if they need to (e.g. Night Moves), others can go properly cross-table
(Kindred Spirits). Other bleed decks can't so easily, of course.

Also, if any vote deck could take such actions cross-table and justify
it on "I have a DU in my deck", that undermines play-to-win anyway.

However, play-to-win is more robust than "Must take the optimal action,
RIGHT NOW." People make mistakes, people miscalculate, and plans get
foiled. ("OMG YOU VOX DOMINI-ED MY DRAMATIC UPHEAVAL I'M DOOMED.")
People can mistakenly make cross-table alliances - only to find
themselves on the pointy end of a shafting.

table is. DU and KR made it possible to completely rearrange this half way
through the game, or whatever. A unique ability.

nicely encourages the stated goal of the game.

*Actually* ousting someone is different from performing an action which may
or may not later contribute to the oust. I can see the relevancy but that's
not quite the same thing.

Using a KRC vote as an example I see the allocation of damage to kill a
player other than your prey as *bad* play, unless the acting player can
demonstrate what's in it for them. Allocating damage which *doesn't* oust is
not so much of an issue because it's not actually ousting anyone. I'm not
saying it's not an issue - you could still argue for bad play but it's more
grey, whereas an oust is very clear cut and it rewards the predator not the
acting player.

player anyway of course, but that's the kind of thing you just have to judge
on the day.

Environmental effects are slightly different though again. They target your
prey *as well* as everybody else, which is a different case from
*specifically and singly* targeting a player other than your prey with an
ousting action. I take umbrage with the latter, not the former.

yet-to-be-seen card to be clutching at straws. I can see though that
ditching DU and KR *does* obviate these kinds of arguments... ;)

Mike

Mike wrote:

> I would argue that Anarch Revolt (when stacked) is the only card capable of
> destroying a whole table. Antedeluvian Awakening and Fame cause similar
> environmental damage but they're one-shot only.

1st Tradition decks, Smiling Jack decks, (moot now, but) table dancers.
I'm sure there are more, but it's really irrelevant because I don't
think you require a "kill the whole table deck" for it to be in your
interest to oust someone else.

I rarely play decks that are built for the sweep. Every now and then
the game just falls out that way, but I'm looking at the game win. Most
generally, collapse the table to a favorable three way, and then win
that three way. It may be counter argued that this is insufficient for
a really large tournament, but A) I don't think the counterargument
holds in the end, as 3 GW are going to get you there, B) we don't all
attend really large tournaments, and C) the constraints tournaments of
that size place on viable deck choices betray their problematic nature, IMO.

Lastly, in a 5 player game, one VP can just go *poof* and it's not
really an impediment towards your own game win. Even very early (and
thus likely to be faulty) speculation about the late game state is
buffered by the fact that you can fuck up once and possibly oust the
wrong guy without irrevocably shooting yourself in the foot. It's a
game of limited information and best guesses must suffice.

> And Anarch Revolt should be addressed by the Rules Team because it *can*
> destroy a whole table. It's a much more serious threat IMHO to the metagame
> and to the predator-prey relationship then any other card I could name.

That's a specific issue with that card, and not really relevant to the
discussion at hand, which is "can I oust cross table and still be
playing to win."

--

David Cherryholmes

When your prey is ousted, you gain a VP and 6 pool. When you are
ousted, your predator gains a VP and 6 pool. Making a deal to gang up
on someone doesn't change this. Going up stream doesn't change this.
Ousting someone X-Table with KRC's doesn't change this. Who *you* need
to oust to get a VP and 6 pool isn't ever changed by deals.

Regardless of what deal you make and how that deal pans out, your prey
is still your prey and your predator is still your predator. DU and KR
*changed* who your (and other folks') preys and predators are. Totally
different.

immediately and instead left them hanging by a thread, you had
significant disincentive to try, as it was very likely that someone
would switch places with you from across the table to steal your VP.

Messages.Author: John Flournoy
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:

> >>Care to link some google/usenet discussion where
> >>this problem was noted and arisen ?

Again, not every discussion occurs over usenet - there are at least a
half-dozen other sizable forums for VTES discussion, including regional
forums like the German and British VTES sites, White Wolf's forum,
thepathofblood.com, and so on.

> Find REAL examples of people discussing these cards in terms of
> a balance problem, not just someone discussing the tactics of
> the game.

Sure. DU/KR has been discussed in several different threads on the Path
of Blood's forums by a large group of players, where a number of
people put both in their 'top 5 most powerful votes' along with
comments about how the vp-snipe aspect made the cards too powerful. It
also came up in a thread about table-balancing and how DU/KR made it
harder to do that (it's hard to use cross-table effects like rushes or
KRC's or whatever to effectively balance a table when the table order
might switch abruptly).

Several people have mentioned at least in passing the disruptive nature
of the cards in clan newsletters, as well.

I'd also suggest looking back at April's 'what to ban' thread in the
newsgroup, where several people mention how they either want to ban
DU/KR or have gotten in the habit of packing Direct Interventions
specifically because of the prevalence of DU/KR in decks.

There was also a usenet discussion in April under 'Protect Whining'
where players discussed the prevalance of Kindred Spirits/Dramatic
Upheaval decks that never bled their prey, instead planning from the
get-go to KS cross-table and then seat-switch, giving the target two
predators in practice. (That style of deck ABSOLUTELY undermines the
prey/predator relationship that LSJ refers to.)
That should be a sufficient start.

> Fred

-John Flournoy

Succubus Club: banned as not appropriate for competitive play. My
interpretation: SC enables Resources of multiple players to be
combined/reallocated in a manner not condusive to competitive play.
Succubus Club enables an environment which circumvents the normal
predator-prey relationship, as leveraged through table deals.

of their own choosing.

Club.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Matthew T. Morgan" <far...@io.com> wrote in messagenews:Pine.LNX.4.44.041207...@fnord.io.com...

> On Tue, 7 Dec 2004, Frederick Scott wrote:
>
>> Find REAL examples of people discussing these cards in terms of
>> a balance problem, not just someone discussing the tactics of
>> the game.
>
> I've only skimmed this thread so please forgive me if this has already
> been mentioned, by why is it important that banning DU and KR was
> discussed on this group?

Three reasons:
1) In most forums there isn't an easy way to get at the history of
the forum, so claiming it's been discussed there is unprovable. Meaning,
I don't think you discount such claims but you can't verify them either
so what are you supposed to do about such a dispute?

2) *We're* here. One issue I think is legimate against the ban (and make
no mistake, I think some of the issues against it are bogus) is that we
got blindsided by it. There was no appreciable discussion about it. If
there was discussion elsewhere, I'd say that's interesting but certainly
the people who hang out here seem to be correct in saying that they've
never had a chance to express an opinion about it because it's never been
raised as an issue here. You don't post to loudly say, "Oh, by the way,
Kindred Restructure and Dramatic Upheavel exist in this game and I think
that's just ducky! Keep 'em!" At least, no one's going to post that
unless someone else (or really a group of someone elses) has taken the
time to loudly post that they want these cards banned.

3) If lots of players are having experiences that make them feel these
cards were a problem, I don't think the discussion about it would be
confined to just one forum. If such discussion were in another forum
but skipped the newsgroup, I think that's pretty sketchy evidence that
the mass population playing the game felt a problem existed.

> In addition to the fact that only a small percentage of VTES players post
> here regularly, I think this group also has a tendency to "group-think"
> (to use a term which of late has been popular to explain the
> inexplicable). If banning those cards isn't on the "group-brain" then
> it's not going to get discussed. It doesn't mean it's a bad idea.

No, it doesn't. But I think you're not as correct about "group-think"
as you say. One thing I notice about the newsgroup is that issues I
consider to be "real" seem to come up over and over - often with new
posters entering the newsgroup posting about them because they hadn't
seen previous discussion. It depends on what you're looking for in the
level of discussion.

I think it's pretty clear that this banning wasn't a response to problem
seen by the general population of card players. It was something else.
I don't automatically think that's wrong. But at least don't say this
has had discussion when it doesn't seem to have had much substantial
discussion. Or it you're going say it happened elsewhere not here, then
that statement could also be more forthright.

> Is it too late to get some discussion in about how seat-switchers should
> be banned?

Obviously not! ;-)

Fred

month,

I'm not disagreeing with that. I offered those comments as a rebuttal
to your statement of "Find REAL examples of people discussing these
cards in terms of a balance problem".

I certainly agree that it wasn't discussed _much_ on Usenet, but it was
an occasional issue, and more importantly, discussions of this nature
have not and do not solely consist of Usenet posts. The subject has
come up on a variety of sites and/or discussions lately, ranging from
usenet, to web forums, to playtest lists (there, I've said it) to
private emails to face-to-face discussions.

> I'm saying you'll have to forgive people who feel blind-sided by the
> banning of these cards because it's really hard to look at the
traffic
> here and see any content which would tend to justify it.

I'm absolutely forgiving of that. Not everybody reads all the various
forums where things like this might get discussed.

I am somewhat less forgiving of people who say (directly quoting
someone else, not you): "no-one complained about them" or "the decision

was uttelrly done in a very arbitrary way".

It just so happened that your statements were somewhat supporting his
easily disproven statements of fact, so that makes it harder to
separate your more reasonable statements from his absolute-statement
falsehoods. Sorry for jumping down your proverbial throat too hard.

--------------

As a side note to all the other people who feel blind-sided because
they didn't see a lot of discussion on usenet ahead of time: other,
much more significant changes to the game have occured in the past with
little to no discussion on the newsgroup; things like the grouping
rule, the adoption of group 4, the inclusion of Bloodlines, Anarchs,
three-way cards, outferiors, Events, the change in card layout, the
decisions about what cards to reprint or not and so on.

Many enormous changes to the game have occured without
publically-archived discussion. Many of these things get specifically,
_privately_ discussed, analyzed and playtested and discussed by
multiple groups of experienced players. Sometimes these things are
adopted, and sometimes they are left out (like the 'double edge' rule
playtested back in the game's beginning.) But just because you don't
see or aren't part of the discussions of changes and/or new things for
the game doesn't mean that no or little discussion has occured.
> Fred

-John Flournoy

Why haven't you looked for yourself? It's not impossible to develop
one's own Google-using skills (even though Google-beta does, I admit,
look kind of nasty right now).

On September 21, 2004, Jo Herroelen (wolflord) mentioned "there are
cards which are a lot more disruptive, and force tables into kingmaking
a lot more than AR (for example Dramatic upheaval or Kindred
Restructure, but nobody's complaining about them are they?)"

http://groups-beta.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/5c464a7fc02314d2

An odd formulation, since he claimed that KR and DU were very disruptive
to the game, but that no one complained about them. But our own Daneel
immediately responded "I do. Complain-complain."

http://groups-beta.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/0b06a7e2d75dcb4b

I then chimed in myself to claim that I complained about Dramatic
Upheaval as well, though admittedly I didn't provide a laundry list of
reasons in that message.

http://groups-beta.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/4e0b8fa9c750093e

Brian White's message has been mentioned already.

Here's one where Charles Lechasseur mentions KR and DU as overpowered
political cards, in July of this year:

http://groups-beta.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/b9e9e5b082d9cce2

Wouter Kuyper agreed with him in the same thread:

http://groups-beta.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/b1dde16b4f063b10

David Cherryholmes, of course, put them in his "what to ban" list in
that thread that mutated from talking about Rotschreck.

If you're looking for hints that this could have been coming, LSJ posted
on the newsgroup in December 2003 saying that "I don't think Succubus
Club is as disruptive as Kindred Restructure or
Dramatic Upheaval."

http://groups-beta.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/24e759b7469a1ac9

I then argued in response that Succubus Club was a little more
disruptive, but that Upheaval and Restructure were also probably
inappropriate for truly competitive play.

http://groups-beta.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/b5e332348694c333

In September of 2001, Andrew S. Davidson pointed out, in a thread
discussing Succubus Club and whether it should be banned, that (at that
time) Kindred Restructure appeared in the TWDA 15 times, and Dramatic
Upheaval 23 times, to Succubus Club's 1 time.

http://groups-beta.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/e110d2a73e19e9c7

In December 2000, Jeff Thompson agreed with a post suggesting that KR/DU
are some of the most powerful effects in the game, and provided a link
to a Paul Johnson article talking about the same thing:

http://groups-beta.google.com/group/rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad/msg/93fbd90ce83adc6b

Sure, most of these aren't discussions specifically about *banning*
Dramatic Upheaval or Kindred Restructure. I believe this is largely
because the players here believe (rightly) that they don't have the
power to get cards banned, and that talking about how much they'd like
to see card X banned isn't all that worthwhile a use of their time.

The other major reason I see for banning Succubus Club, Dramatic
Upheaval, and Kindred Restructure *now* is that competitive play is
(from my point of view) bigger now than it has ever been in the past.
For most of VTES history, most tournaments have been fairly small and
local. Only recently has an organized system of qualifier tournaments
and continental championships been developed. In that environment,
cards that disrupt the predator-prey relationship are, I absolutely
agree, not suited for competitive play.

As for getting blind-sided by it, sure. I certainly was. But I think
we ought to expect to be blind-sided (though I agree that it would be
nice if we *did* get some kind of advance notice, or request for
comments, or whatever) by bannings, errata, and so on: that's how it's
always been. The rules authorities don't operate in public and they
don't usually tell us what they're thinking about doing.

Josh

>> Vote decks can throw damage cross-table. Rush decks can throw rushes

>
>*Actually* ousting someone is different from performing an action which may
>or may not later contribute to the oust. I can see the relevancy but that's
>not quite the same thing.

Depends on the set-up. There are lots of times in games where you can
see that someone is, say, using their vampires to block with and leaving
them untapped etc. So if you rush the untapped vampires, suddenly they
end up with no bleed defence.

Sure, someone else (the predator) takes an action here - but the
difference can often be "I acted, he acted" vs "He acted, I acted".
Which in the grand scheme of things, isn't *that* much difference.

Deals can, of course, be broken - but people don't have to break them,
and lots of people keep them.

>Using a KRC vote as an example I see the allocation of damage to kill a
>player other than your prey as *bad* play, unless the acting player can
>demonstrate what's in it for them.

In a Dramatic Upheaval deck, it's obvious what's in it for me - cross-
table damage to someone who can't block, letting me move in with the DU.
(Or KR - but DU is generally better, IME.)

>Allocating damage which *doesn't* oust is
>not so much of an issue because it's not actually ousting anyone.

That's surely not true.

If I do 9 damage to you with 3 KRCs, that's not much of an issue? It
puts you on 1 pool, and that's not much of an issue? Urr... Why are
things only an issue if they actually perform the oust?

Assume that you have a predator with 2 vampires. He's not playing much
(any?) Fortitude, so you calculate for his worst two bleeds. He's only
been playing Computer Hacking, so you've gone for weenie defence. And
you can block him, probably. So you can stand up to him, and are
discarding your (say) combat defence. It's weenie bleed, you're not
about to die from combat.

But I DU in (and I was your grand-prey) and oust you. You had two other
people to consider before me (your grand-pred and your pred), so you
really weren't thinking about defending properly against me just yet -
it wasn't like I was about to roll the two of them over.

Do you think that - even if you allow the turn to end RIGHT NOW - that
any deck can suddenly alter the course it's been taking, the cards it's
been discarding, the pro-active defence it's been taking etc.?

>> Add Fame, if you need the actual killing blow.
>
>Environmental effects are slightly different though again. They target your
>prey *as well* as everybody else,

I'm thinking of the "Burn three pool" effect of Fame here. Very few
decks ever get to exploit the 1 a turn. Someone typically rescues it or
burns it - an ally if they don't want the pool loss, the aggressor if
they want the vampire burned (too troublesome to leave around, e.g.
Arika). There's also "Tension in the Ranks", which is somewhat weaker
IMO but still usable if you like that sort of thing.

>which is a different case from
>*specifically and singly* targeting a player other than your prey with an
>ousting action.

Which you can still do. Political decks, rush decks, bleed decks can
all target one player and do pool loss.

>> Also, if any vote deck could take such actions cross-table and justify
>> it on "I have a DU in my deck", that undermines play-to-win anyway.
>
>Possibly. Personally I would see the reliance of the draw of a single
>yet-to-be-seen card to be clutching at straws. I can see though that
>ditching DU and KR *does* obviate these kinds of arguments.

What if there are five in the deck? Eight?

How many does it need before you can say "Right, do what you want?"

winning

> I think that no, we would not find reasonable numbers
> justifying such decision.

It'd be impossible for someone to say 'how many decks have won by the
use of a specific card' since not all tournaments report examples of
play, so here are some numbers on card inclusion:

I skimmed every deck in the Tournament Winning Deck Archive that has
won in 2004.

I found 20 decks that I'd consider 'vote decks', and of those 20, 15
had DU, KR or both, most of which had multiples.

Additionally, I found 13 decks that had which I would not call a vote
deck yet had vote cards (1-6 political cards, plus 1 Baltimore purge
deck with 9 votes backing it up) and 9 of those 13 included DU/KR.
Several had nothing _but_ seat-switching votes.

So by my preliminary count of decks that won tourneys that I could
quickly identify as having ANY votes in them at all in 2004 (excluding
storyline tourneys), 24 of 33 decks had either KR or DU or both in
them, and more than half the vote decks had 2 to 5 copies.

I would certainly think that if you're putting multiple copies of a
card in your deck, you're intending to at least have the opportunity to
play it. There will certainly be times when playing a KR/DU in hand is
not optimal in a given game, but over half the winning political decks
PLANNED to be able to seat switch and about 70% made a point to include
it.

(Anecdotally, at least 2 of the 5 finalists at this year's NAC packed
DU/KR, and Hughues Bertrand (who came in second) has mentioned in his
analysis of his play that he based decisions on his planned ability to
seat-switch later in the game, which he did pull off once.)

(Also anecdotally, I won a storyline tournament within the last month
solely because I managed to VP-snipe a VP the turn before my prey
could, and we were both planning for much of the game to use the card
in such fashion. And I felt so very dirty doing it! :P )

As to whether having over 2/3 of the winning political decks over the
last year include seat-switching is a problem or not, that's up to the
individual.

Fred, you're STILL using generalizations like 'the player population'
that aren't accurate in spirit or in fact.

The people who have been complaining in person, in private emails, in
playtest groups, over other web forums, and even (rarely) on this
newsgroup are people who play the game. They're not mystery WW
employees who've never played V:TES, they are as much part of 'the
player population' as you or I are.

The example changes I listed were DECIDEDLY run past 'the player
population' before being introduced to the game. Pretty much every one
of them (maybe not card layout, shrug) was run through multiple
playtest groups, and those playtest groups have been comprised of some
of the most active and/or sizable and/or high-quality playgroups out
there.

They were not run past EVERY MEMBER of the 'player population', and
they were not run past the usenet group as a subset of the player base,
because (like almost every CCG company and most game companies) the
reward for letting EVERY player playtest a game is that you get
overwhelmed with requests and opinions from people who are not worth
listening to.

For example, there are people who post to this usenet group on a
regular basis who haven't actually played the game in several years,
who admit they don't know the rules or cards, and yet feel compelled to
give their input on strategy, rules and game design issues. Those
people's opinions aren't worth the time it takes you to killfile them.

So instead, White Wolf usually makes a point to start by going out and
proactively soliciting the opinions of specific players and groups of
players about things like upcoming changes, instead of throwing open
the gates to everyone with a web browser and an opinion. (If you look
on usenet, you'll find that people occasionally ask how they can
playtest the R0XX0R new cards and are told that White Wolf solicits the
playtesters from the player base, not the other way around.)

And on some occasions, they _do_ solicit the opinions of the wider
player population, such as when LSJ asked for suggestions for themes
for new expansions that players wanted to see last December on multiple
forums (which is partly responsible for us getting a Kindred Most
Wanted set), or the repeated statements of 'if you guys can come up
with a way to fix this problem card/rule, please do so because the
options already considered aren't workable' for a variety of cards -
including DR/KU.

I'm actually pleased to see LSJ posting asking for people to suggest
ways to fix DU/KR to take them back off the banned list; the game does
have a history of banning a problem card in the short term while asking
for more and more input on how to fix it in the long-term. Even if that
doesn't always work.

(There's also the whole side issue of copyrights and NDAs for truly new
material and their specifics; hard to get 'usenet and everyone who can
search google' to sign off on an NDA so you can solicit specific
feedback from all the players on a new card before its published - but
that's not really relevant when talking solely about rules changes like
banning cards.)

I've been told (by people in a position to know) that people who make a
point to be involved in discussions on the newsgroup, talk about
strategies, card balance, rules changes and so forth - like you are
doing now, and don't get me wrong, I'm not at all suggesting you
shouldn't be griping about how you feel left out of the process and why
that bugs you - are much more likely to be included in the people whose
opinions get solicited, who get to playtest, etc etc. People who show a
desire and a commitment to improving the quality of the game and
demonstrate the ability to hold intelligent discussions on it get
noticed by the people who look for player input on big decisions. (I
won't claim that they all get consulted on every decision, but their
chances of being included in any one discussion is certainly
astromically higher than a random member of the player population.)

I completely understand and sympathize with how you feel about being
blind-sided by this change. Lots of players were. I even to some degree
sympathize with your being upset that the discussions (which do happen)
don't generally take place where you might find them or take part.

I do take exception to your generalizations that the changes now or in
the past were not asked for, not discussed, and that 'the player
population' had no input either specifically this time or as an ongoing
pattern, because that simply is not true. They weren't discussed by
everyone or in front of everyone, but they were discussed (often at
length) by a number of the most involved and experienced players of the
game.

> I don't really think that's good. Sometimes it may be necessary but
> it isn't a good thing. And the fact that White Wolf chooses to do it
> certainly doesn't make it good, either. (That last is pointed out
> because it seems like you're using the fact that it happened in the
> past to justify it. Perhaps you didn't mean it that way.)

You're right, I didn't mean that as a justification, since 'White Wolf
chooses to make changes without consulting the player population' isn't
what I was suggesting. If that were the case, I'd agree with you that
it's bad.

And even if the decisions WERE being made in a vaccuum, it's nice to
see the designer(s) saying 'here's a surprise change, now please feel
free to tell us better alternatives cause we'll consider reversing it
if you find one that works' rather than a final fait accompli from the
get-go.

> Fred

-John Flournoy

Neither of these fix the fundemental problem of the cards--namely that they
allow a player to not have to focus on ousting *their* prey, 'cause they can
choose to oust anyone else at the table that happens to be easy to oust for
whatever reason.

The designers and tournament authority clearly seem interested in refocusing
the game on its intended goal--kill your prey, that being the guy sitting to
your left when the game starts. DU and KR both completely circumvent this.
There is nothing at all to stop a deck using, say, DU or KR from simply
sitting on its resources and protecting itself till, say, its prey (who has
been unmolested up till this point and likely plowing ahead at high speed)
is close to ousting your Grandprey. And then you steal your Prey's seat,
oust your Grandprey-now Prey, gain a VP and 6 extra pool. And then do it
again to whomever is closest to being ousted. And so on. This gives a *huge*
benefit to someone who is completely ignoring what is supposed to be the
fundemantal guiding focus of the game--kill your prey.

Can you see how this could be deemed inappropriate to the game where the
main goal is supposed to be "kill your prey"? And how errata isn't going to
fix that?

Succubus Club is banned. I'd lay money, however, that a new card that has a
similar effect (allows folks to trade stuff) but is greatly restricted will
be printed eventually. 'Cause while SC is also wildly inappropriate for
competetive play, it *is* a card that could be fixed by errata, 'cause the
inappropriateness of the effect of the card isn't the effect in and of
itself (i.e. trading stuff), it is the scale at which it is possible. It
seems very likely that there is some version of a SC type card possible that
allows players to trade some stuff but isn't capable of 'causing endless
havok, like SC is.

DU and KR? Unless the errata to these cards prevents them from being used to
switch seats, the errata isn't fixing the problem. And if the errata does
prevent them from being used to switch seats, then they aren't the same
cards and there is no point to the errata.

Messages.Author: Xian

On Sat, 04 Dec 2004 02:17:14 GMT, LSJ <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote:

>The Banned List is expanded to include three cards that are
>not suited for competitive play: Dramatic Upheaval, Kindred
>Restructure, and Succubus Club.

Awesome. An excellent decision, I think.

While I understand that people are frustrated about this decision (and
I realize I'm coming to the argument late), there's something I think
that hasn't been touched upon (much).

The predator/prey mechanic is fairly distinct (or at least was, I'm
not very up on my CCGs) to V:tES, and in the CCGs I'm familiar with,
seating doesn't really matter very much (Shadowfist, Magic, Babylon5).
V:tES, by placing some sort of emphasis on seating, has made seating
important to the players (possibly more important than it should be).
The ability to change seating is also relatively distinct in V:tES,
and made more important because it can matter.

In a "friendly" game, DU/KR are minor annoyances, and rather
characteristic of Garfield's desire to throw some sort of monkeywrench
into every aspect of the game, and increase some of the
parlor-game-like attributes of V:tES. See also: Cunctator Motation,
Curse of Nitocris, Malkavian Prank, Monocle of Clarity.

In games that have an outcome that "matters", though, DU/KR supplant
the randomness of seating with an order that only benefits one (or
perhaps two) players, to the detriment of the other players, and it
imposes a new state on the game that cannot easily be undone. As
someone (can't recall who) pointed out, there is a "before DU/KR"
state, and an "after DU/KR" state which are fundamentally different.
The ability to change the table that much, and with such devestating
effect gives unprecedented power to political decks, which is simply
undesirable, even if that mechanism could be used by all archetypes.

If the following card existed:

Bum's Rush++
Action
+1 stealth
(D) Enter combat with a minion. If this minion inflicts more damage
than the opposing minion in the resulting combat, burns the opposing
minion, or sends the opposing vampire to torpor, this methuselah may
switch seats with any other methuselah at the table.

that effect would likely be deemed problematic by many (most?)
players.

But in effect, that is what DU does. DU picks a "fight" that it can
probably win (Bewitching Oration/Awe/Cryptic Rider/Business
Pressure/etc.), and gets a large effect out of it. Sure, the above
isn't exactly the same, but it's similar. The targeted methuselah can
block it instead of predator/prey, combat defense exists (and is
actually more varied than vote defense), and not all methuselahs have
a say in the outcome. But I think the point is still valid.

Feel free to discuss. Or not. There have already been a lot of
messages on the subject, and I think most of you have already made up
your minds (for good or ill).

Xian

I wouldn't say that seat-switching has 'suddenly' become a problem. I'd
say it's something that has _gradually_ become a problem, as more and
more players realized what they could do with the mechanic and started
to use it accordingly in increasing numbers in tournaments.

I also wouldn't say it's 'every time a political deck has won', but it
has become increasingly frequent to use KR/DU specifically to snipe
VPs; multiple players in the last 6 months have discussed in tournament
reports and/or casual conversation how in the course of winning (or
making the finals) they've 'sat back and waited for someone to be weak
enough to seat-switch to steal the vp' instead of making any effort to
oust their prey.

Sometimes those people win, and sometimes they just get VP, but more
and more often of late the cards have been included in decks with the
intent of engineering cross-table VP sniping instead of other purposes
(like avoiding a horrific predator, which is a separate, yet still
undesirable effect.)

> Emiliano

-John Flournoy

Consider:

In some situations, the power of a card is readily obvious. For
instance, as-printed Return to Innocence is hugely powerful. This was
obvious from the start. Having to take steps against it was something
that was obvious the moment you saw it. Well, maybe not quite then.
You'd think "Ooh, it burns the vampire. That's not good." And then
people would discuss how you can get round that being a problem and...
well, you see how it quickly becomes a hot card.

However, another card may not be registering on people's radar, but may
slowly start to take on a more central role as more and more people just
start including it. People take steps to account for it in some ways,
and it's not a radical sea-change like RtoI. But at some point, you
could see it as problematic that if people aren't preparing for it
specifically, they get screwed.

I am not entirely convinced of this, but it strikes me as one possible
way to see how this works.

I'd include a few of the reprint changes in Camarilla Edition as having
worked in a similar-ish fashion.

Just a little historical side note...

Richard Garfield pointed out that one reason for the predator/prey

relationship was to give players an idea of who their short term
opponents are.

Also, if my memory is correct, I recall him saying that he only wanted
players to earn VPs for ousting thier prey. He likened getting VPs for
ousting players other than your predator or prey to early roleplaying
experiences where the player that landed the death blow to the dragon
received the experience points for the kill (even if other players did

99% of the work). Jyhad would be different in that if you ousted
someone other than your prey, you'd be doing it for some other benefit
(not VPs).

IMO, DU/KR fly in the face of those concepts. Claims that you are still

ousting your prey after a DU/KR might technically be true but violates
the spirit in which the concept was created--that the player who does
99% of the work shouldn't be robbed of a VP by the player who deals the
death blow (1%).

-Robert

>>If one player is suposed to "gun for" his prey why are there cards
such
as Kindred Spirits allowing to bleed other players other than your prey

then? Or votes such as KRC? They undermine "the gun for", too.>>

No, they don't. Using Kindred Spirits or KRC to kill someone X-table
doesn't get *you* a VP. It gives someone else a VP. Consequently, there
is built in disnicentive to do these things--X-table actions tend to
make you weaker and someone else stronger. And they never get you a VP,
which is your main incentive to do anything in game.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Enrique San Martín Woerner wrote:

> if you are saying
> that in an infinetisimal moment, each player don't have a player to "gun
> for", you are entering in a philosophical discution's of the duration of
> the minimal moment...

Ok. When you sit down to play a game of VTES, you sit next to 2 other
people. One of the is your predator. One of them is your prey. Once this
relationship is established, your job is to kill your prey--the game has
significant built in incentive to do this--if you kill *your* prey, i.e. the
guy you sat next to when the game started, you get a VP and 6 pool. As 6
pool is a lot of pool, and you win the game by getting, generally, at least
3 VPs, this is a very significant, concrete incentive to kill your prey (as
opposed to someone elses prey).

What this sets up is a situation where the whole game dynamic revolves
around you killing your prey (they guy to your immediate left) and your
predator killing you. When you introduce an element into the situation that
allows you to arbitrarily change who your prey is (i.e. Dramatic Upheaval,
say), you no longer have any concrete incentive to kill your prey--you can
kill *anyone's* prey, and get the 1 VP and 6 pool. You don't have to operate
within the established main relationship of the game--predator/prey, as you
can make anyone your prey at any time, making the whole structure moot.

Currently, there are a lot of actions you can do cross table--Rush, Kindred
Spirits, Eagle's Sight block, toss KRC damage, whatever. But doing these
things to someone who is not your prey comes with significant
disadvantages--you are using your resources (actions, blood, cards,
whatever) to make someone *else's* life easier--someone else gets to benefit
from your action, likely, much more than you do, as it makes it easier for
that someone else to oust their prey. Which is what the main goal of the
game is (oust your prey). When you can switch seats at a whim, these cross
table actions lose their balance, and the whole game loses it's main
governing principal (i.e. kill your prey).

Enrique San Martín Woerner wrote:

> Name: Any name...

See, making specific hoser cards is rarely the answer. This card is
generally less effective than simply using Vox Domini (the cancel a vote
card). And even then, having a specific way to stop a given card does not
make it ok to have in the game if the effect is inappropriate--again, look
back that the imaginary political action "I win!' which when it passes,
automatically ousts your prey. There are ways to stop this card (intercept,
Vox Domini, Delaying Tactics, voting it down, whatever). That doesn't mean
it is ok to make such a card.

Look at Return to Innocence. That was stopable as well. It could be blocked,
bounced, or Archon Investigated. But its effect was simply inappropriate for
the game, so it was banned.

DU and KR are simply inappropriate effects. It doesn't matter that they can
be stopped, blocked, voted down, Delaying Tacticed, or whatever. They are
still simply inappropriate effects. Consequently, no amount of errata or
silver bullets will make them ok.

> Banning card's it's not the solution, the posibility of play an
> non-competive card(s) can be reduced to 1% or less, if you make cards
> like that, you kill undirect some card(s) and give to the players to

whatever.

> would be fine or some like that)

There is no errata that will fix the cards. The effect is simply not
appropriate for the game.

> Why in Black Hand in one of the preconstructed deck's you put DU???,
> what be done with that card???, would be replace via mail exchange
> progamam???

Dude. The Black Hand starters were designed and printed before they decided
to ban the card. And the cards are still perfectly playable in casual
play--just not tournament play.

And as mentined before, a mail exchange? Dude--there are plenty of cards
that when you pull them out of a booster are essentially unplayable. If you
are playing draft, you end up with lots of cards you can't play. If you open
a booster and get, like, Open Grate, are you putting that in your deck
immediately? What about a clan specific master to a clan you don't use? Do
you need a trade in program for that as well?

It is a card. In a collectible card game. Sometimes, cards are made
unplayable. It is one of the risks of the format. And we all deal and move
on.

My, how time flies. Anyway, this was hardly a call for these cards to
be banned. Later that month I suggested that Bum Rush ought to be
banned and made a strong, albeit tongue-in-cheek, argument for doing
so. Banning Bum Rush would make more sense to me than banning KR and
DU.

TCG turns out to have been unsuitable for competitive play all this
time. There's another multiplayer TCG celebrating its 10th
anniversary soon: Shadowfist. Those who like serious competitive play
should note that that game has no banned cards, not a single one. It
will get a new base set next year, but all the old cards should still
be legal. And I don't expect that they will monkey with the card
backs or layout either. So, if you want to change seats in that game,
you can play your 1996 "Year of the Rat" card without anyone crying
foul.

Andrew

For many years I've been playing an abandoned game without really caring
about how many poeple play it. Arguments like "but nobody plays VTES"
bounced off me simply because I knew the game was worth playing. I would
have continued to collect the game even if everybody I know have had
stopped playing. Drawing a parallel between the popularity and quality
of the game did not appeal to me back then; I might as well just stick
to that approach. The growing player base is a result of popularity. The

more a sign of quality, if anything can be. Yet I would advise against
the high horse. VTES is not the best CCG. It is a good and well-supported

with MRH, JA and KRC than with the current crew. Maybe LSJ can be
included with the benefactors if he had no saying in the layout change,
because the game really gained rules-wise, errata-wise and cards-wise.

tendency.

perfect quality control detract from the purple haze.

they probably wouldn't pick VTES... Example 2, it is exceedingly rare to
find a regular Shadowfist group, outside a few major markets. If being able
to find a group to play with easily is a criteria for your "best CCG",

booster sets that was in production for many years, and they still run
tournaments and have a fan base and THEY don't have any banned cards
either.

I guess that makes Spellfire an excellent-quality and well-designed CCG
that isn't a joke and worthy of consideration of 'best CCGs'?

I would be surprised if V:TES made charts like this even when a new
expansion first hits. Past polling that I'm aware of revolved around
questions posed to a handful of retailers. Frankly, V:TES has not been
very big in the retail world for a long time (and for a variety of
reasons). Look at Potomac Distribution's ads they mail out and notice
the prominence of V:TES displays when an expansion is due out. A large
percentage of V:TES sales (I'd guess over 50%) are made through online
sales of one kind or another. Also, nearly 1/2 of the sales are
probably made overseas. Somehow I doubt the Scrye offices were on the
phone with game stores in Budapest and Paris. :)
